title: Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian?
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Mediterranean Travels
description: Compare one part at a time across the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian orders, then classify twelve column features and buildings from our route.

learningObjectives: Classify twelve described column features and buildings from our route as Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.
prerequisites: The Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian orders (Chapter 10, Part Three)

dependencies: None; reuses the column drawing of the Three Classical Orders poster (docs/posters/column-types/orders-columns.png) by relative path

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Explore-then-classify: compare one part across three labeled columns, then sort twelve feature and building cards with immediate feedback
keyQuestions: What does the top of a column tell you?
Which parts separate Doric from the other two orders, and which part separates Ionic from Corinthian?
Why are the buildings of Ionia Ionic?
commonMisconceptions: Any capital with scrolls is Corinthian; scrolls without acanthus leaves are Ionic.
Fluting names the order on its own; Ionic and Corinthian share the same 24-flute pattern.
All Greek temples are Doric; the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the first giant Ionic temples.
Smooth, unfluted shafts belong to one order; they occur in all three.
assessmentOpportunities: First-attempt score on twelve cards (mastery: 10 of 12).
On site: name what can and cannot be said about a column that has lost its capital.
